PBC Linear

Design, manufacturing, and automation work from my summer 2026 internship at PBC Linear in Roscoe, IL.

Uniguide rail redesign & bearing trays

PBC Linear internship, summer 2026. SolidWorks, GD&T, DFM, Keyence measurement.

PBC Linear needed a D125 Uniguide rail assembly (a carriage slides along a rail to move a load in a straight line) that would work with one of its existing product lines. Separately, the shop floor needed a better way to store its linear bearings.

I engineered a custom rail, carriage, and lead screw in SolidWorks and added a hand crank on one end so the carriages can be moved by hand. For the bearings, I modeled a set of trays, each sized for one bearing size with a pocket for every bearing.

The result was a rail assembly that fits the existing product line, plus trays that keep more than 100 bearings organized and easy to count instead of loose in bins.

Claw machine demonstrator

PBC Linear intern project. SolidWorks, FDM 3D printing, linear actuators.

PBC Linear wanted a claw machine to show off its linear actuators, with one actuator moving the claw side to side (X axis) and another raising and lowering it (Z axis). I built it with four other interns. Partway through, the X-axis actuator was moving far slower than it should, and the claw struggled to hold on to prizes.

I tracked down what was holding the actuator back, and I designed and 3D printed three parts: new claw hooks, a rope attachment, and a section of the prize holder.

The X-axis speed went from 0.15 to 0.45 m/s, three times faster, and with the new hooks the claw picked up prizes about 40% more often.

Actuator swivel bracket

PBC Linear internship, summer 2026. SolidWorks, machined in-house.

One of PBC Linear’s linear actuators, a long enclosed rail with a carriage riding along it, needed a solid way to be mounted without getting in the way of that motion. My task was to design a bracket to hold and support it.

I modeled a U-shaped cradle that the actuator sits down into, with raised ribs along the inside floor to locate it and a round pin on each side wall so the bracket can pivot. I built it as a single part in SolidWorks, mirroring the features across the center plane and filleting the edges, then submitted a build request to PBC Linear’s in-house machine shop.

The machinists made the bracket from my design, giving the actuator a mount that holds it in place and lets it tilt to the angle it needs instead of being locked flat.

Suh Lab Research

The Suh Lab, led by Professor Youngjoon Suh, studies multiphase heat transfer: boiling, condensation, and the thermal management problems behind electronics cooling and energy systems. I’m on the team that designed and built the lab’s flow-boiling test loop.

How the loop works

A piston pump drives coolant through a Coriolis flowmeter and an in-line heater into the test section, where it boils on a heated copper surface. A condenser returns it to liquid before it flows back to the reservoir.

The return line conditions the fluid before it reaches the pump again: a degassing unit removes dissolved gas, and an in-line filter and Y-type strainer catch debris. An accumulator on a 3-way valve damps pressure pulses from the piston pump, and a separate fluid tank refills the reservoir without opening the loop.

From model to bench

What I did

Before buying or cutting anything, the team needed a full layout of the loop, and once it was on the bench, every piece of equipment had to line up.

I modeled the major components in SolidWorks (reservoir, piston pump, Coriolis flowmeter, in-line heater, test section, and condenser) and chose fitting sizes and materials for every connection. Because the equipment sits at different heights, I designed 3D-printed mounts and leveling bases for the pump, flowmeter, and other pieces, and we set the layout up as a modular configuration. To print those mounts in-house, I also got the lab’s out-of-service Ender 3 working again by replacing a faulty Z-axis limit switch.

Building from the model cut assembly time by about 38%, and the loop came out leak-free. Every flow connection lines up within 4 mm, and the modular layout makes the setup about 25% more repeatable.

Projects

Pump-housing cover thermal redesign

ME 396, Senior Design I. Ansys Mechanical, SolidWorks.

A pump-housing cover on a motorcycle sits right where a rider’s leg can touch it, and it is bolted to an engine that runs hot. The task was to redesign it so no touchable surface goes above 40 °C in still air, the comfort limit from ASTM C1055.

I built a steady-state thermal model in Ansys Mechanical, with the engine mounts held at 90 °C and 60 °C and still-air convection on the outside. The original aluminum cover reached almost 90 °C, and switching to polyethylene only brought it down to about 80 °C, so a material change alone wasn’t enough. I redesigned the cover in SolidWorks with a polyethylene outer shell that stands off from the hot surface, so the part a rider touches isn’t in direct contact with the heat.

The hottest touchable point dropped to 38.2 °C, a 57% drop that meets the 40 °C limit, and the average exposed surface fell to about 27 °C. I checked the result with an energy balance on the mesh and flagged that polyethylene is only rated for 80 °C continuous use, so the 90 °C mount needs a closer look in a design review.

Robot actuator cooling coil

ME 396, Senior Design I. Ansys Fluent, Steady-State Thermal, Static Structural.

The motor in a robot’s shoulder joint runs at about 80 °C and needs to be cooled by a two-turn copper coil (3/8 in tube) wrapped around it. The task was to pick a coolant and flow rate that remove the heat without needing a big pump, and to check that the coil itself holds up.

I compared 9 designs: water, 40% propylene glycol, and a light paraffin oil, each at three flow speeds (Reynolds numbers of 1,000, 100,000, and 10 million). Each one went through a linked chain in Ansys Workbench: Fluent solved the coolant flow and heat transfer, a steady-state thermal model took the temperatures, and a structural model calculated stress. Before trusting the results, I checked them against hand calculations, matching mass flow within 1.6% and heat input within about 0.3%.

The high-speed cases needed tens of thousands of liters per minute, far beyond anything that fits on a robot, so I recommended 40% propylene glycol at the low speed: about 1.6 L/min at a 1.3 kPa pressure drop, which a small onboard pump can handle. The coil’s curvature also boosted heat transfer 2.6 to 3.2 times over a straight tube. The structural results showed that no design met the required safety factor of 2, but the coil itself stayed under 3 MPa; the 300+ MPa peak was at the two rigidly clamped ends, where thermal expansion has nowhere to go. A hand calculation confirmed it, and I recommended flexible hose or small expansion loops at the ends to fix it.

Go-kart chassis

UIC ASME, engine and frame subteam. SolidWorks, welding, 3D printing.

UIC ASME’s engine and frame subteam was building a custom go-kart, and the club also needed rules for its go-kart competition.

I helped design the chassis in SolidWorks and worked on fitting a Tillotson 212 engine (9+ HP) to the frame, choosing parts that worked together. I also helped write the competition rules, putting the safety and spec checks into one standard list.

Drivable couch

UIC ASME, co-lead. SolidWorks, custom fabrication.

Yes, it’s a couch with an engine. UIC ASME set out to turn an old couch into a drivable vehicle. As co-lead, I ran the steering team of five-plus people, and the project also needed money for its main components.

We stripped the couch down to its bare wooden frame and built a new lumber base underneath to carry the drivetrain: a small gas engine with a chain drive to the rear axle, and a rack-and-pinion steering setup with tie rods to the front wheels. My team chose and bought the steering axle and its hardware, balancing what would fit, what would be safe at speed, and what we could build in the club’s shop. I also helped organize fundraisers.

The fundraisers brought in over $800 for the main components, and the engine, chain drive, and steering are now mounted in the new base, with the couch frame going back on top as the seat.

Fidget keyboard cube

ME 347. SolidWorks, FDM 3D printing, MakerSpace.

For ME 347, I set out to design a pocket-sized 5-key keyboard fidget toy that folds into a cube and prints in one piece, with no assembly.

I designed custom spring key switches and 8 print-in-place hinges in SolidWorks, then iterated on tolerances. The first print was too small for the springs to form, and the second printed cleanly but the hinges were too loose.

The final design fixed both problems, and the toy now folds into a cube straight off the printer.

Tennis ball launcher

College of DuPage engineering final. Creo, AutoCAD, welding.

For our final engineering project at College of DuPage, six of us had a $100 budget to build a tennis ball launcher.

We went with a spring-loaded design: a compression spring inside a PVC barrel, mounted on an adjustable pivot, with a repurposed stop-sign pole as part of the structure. I designed a compact 3 ft by 3 ft frame in Creo and AutoCAD, and we tuned the barrel alignment and pivot angle.

The frame used about 93% less material than our first concept, the spring-and-barrel setup made shots about 57% more consistent, and the tuning increased our range by about 83%.
